candidates.attacker_control: The subject/issuer strings come from X509CertSelector/X509CertStoreSelector/X509CRLSelector API state (e.g., setSubject(String)/setIssuerNames), which applications commonly populate from untrusted input (user-supplied DN, e-mail address, name). parseDN only trims DN syntax (attribute name, '=' and ',' boundaries) and does not remove LDAP filter metacharacters, so a value such as 'x)(|(objectClass=*))' survives and is spliced into the filter executed by ctx.search().
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Returned certificates/CRLs are re-checked with xselector.match(cert) / xselector.match(crl) before being returned, so injection alone does not cause an unrelated certificate to be accepted by the selector; the LDAP URL, baseDN and searched attribute names come from application configuration, not from the attacker, which bounds the injection to the filter expression. No escaping/sanitization helper exists elsewhere in the tree that these paths are expected to call, and no validation of the subject string occurs between the selector and the filter concatenation.
candidates.impact: An attacker who can influence the selector value changes the LDAP query semantics executed with the application's bind credentials: the query can be broadened or narrowed, can cause the directory to return certificate/CRL values from entries that the intended filter would not select (information disclosure within the directory's search scope), and can force expensive subtree/wildcard searches (resource-exhaustion/DoS). Because the same class also throws CertStoreException/StoreException on malformed filters, injected syntax can drive error paths.
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses the BC LDAP-backed store (CertStore.getInstance("LDAP", X509LDAPCertStoreParameters), or X509Store "CERTIFICATE/LDAP" / "CERTIFICATE PAIR/LDAP" / "CRL/LDAP" / "ATTRIBUTECERTIFICATE/LDAP" which use LDAPStoreHelper) and builds the selector's subject/issuer from attacker-influenced input. The LDAP URL/baseDN/search attribute names are application configuration; the attacker only controls the filter value.
candidates.root_cause: Both LDAP directory implementations build LDAP filters by direct string concatenation of caller-supplied DN-derived values. In X509LDAPCertStoreSpi.search a filter is built as attributeName + "=" + attributeValue, where attributeValue is "*" + parseDN(subject, ...) + "*" (the selector's subject/issuer), and is then embedded in "(&(" + filter + ")(" + attr + "=*))" and passed to DirContext.search. In LDAPStoreHelper.search the same pattern is used: filter += "(" + attributeNames[i] + "=" + attributeValue + ")". No escaping of LDAP filter metacharacters ('*', '(', ')', '\\', NUL) or rejection of them exists anywhere in the tree (searches for escapeFilter/RFC2254 returned nothing), so filter syntax supplied through the selector survives into the executed query.
candidates.title: LDAP filter injection via unescaped X.509 selector values in LDAP CertStore/LDAPStoreHelper
candidates.trace: X509CertSelector.getSubjectAsString()/getSubjectAsBytes()/getCertificate() -> certSubjectSerialSearch (X509LDAPCertStoreSpi.java:235-261) -> parseDN (line 260) -> search(attrName, "*"+attrValue+"*", attrs) (line 261) -> filter = attributeName + "=" + attributeValue (line 411) -> filter2 = "(&("+filter+")("+temp[0]+"=*))" (line 432) -> ctx.search(params.getBaseDN(), filter2, constraints) (lines 437-438). For CRLs the issuer goes through the same path (lines 346-367). In LDAPStoreHelper the selector subject/issuer reaches search(...) at lines 228, 294, 389 and 461, where filter += "("+attributeNames[i]+"="+attributeValue+")" (line 503) is embedded in filter3 (line 514) and executed at line 536.
candidates.unverified: Whether this exact root cause corresponds to the dataset's ground-truth fix/CVE could not be verified from source (no upstream diff, CVE mapping, tests, or runtime execution is available in this run). The practical exploitability (LDAP server behavior, ACLs, post-search selector matching) was reasoned about only from the source, not demonstrated. The two classes share one root cause (missing filter escaping) and are reported as a single candidate.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-90 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an LDAP Query ('LDAP Injection')

coverage_summary: Tools used: get_source_scope, list_files (3816 visible files; binaries excluded), search_code and bounded read_file. Modules surveyed: core (crypto engines/encodings/signers/ASN.1), prov (JCE RSA/DSA/EC, keystores, LDAP CertStore), pkix (CMS, operator/bc and operator/jcajce, cert path validation, EST), tls (old crypto.tls and new org.bouncycastle.tls TLS API), pg and mail. I traced selector input to the LDAP filter construction in both LDAP implementations, and checked the RSA/PKCS#1, TLS premaster, CMS signature-verification, keystore MAC, XMSS deserialisation and SM2 code paths for counterevidence. Test sources are not present in the snapshot (no core/src/test, prov/src/test, etc.), so test-based corroboration was impossible; build files and release notes were used only as version/state context. Coverage is review-level sampling, not exhaustive line-by-line review of all 3816 files.
limitations: No runtime execution, LDAP server, differential build or upstream/history comparison was available, so the candidate is a source-evidence lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
The snapshot contains no test sources and no VCS history, so I could not identify the immediate fix commit, its CVE, or which of several 1.60-era fixes this tree precedes.

Impact of the LDAP injection is bounded by the post-search selector match and by the fact that returned attributes are the configured certificate/CRL attributes; only query manipulation, possible directory information exposure and DoS were established from source.

Large parts of the repository (provider algorithm wrappers, ASN.1 classes, PGP/mail, TLS record layer) were inspected by targeted search rather than exhaustively, so other issues may exist outside the paths reviewed.

rejected_leads.lead: Unblinded RSA private-key decryption in the lightweight CMS key unwrapper (pkix/src/main/java/org/bouncycastle/operator/bc/BcRSAAsymmetricKeyUnwrapper.java:20 returns new PKCS1Encoding(new RSAEngine()), unlike TLS/PGP/JCE paths that use RSABlindedEngine), plus padding failures converted to OperatorException at BcAsymmetricKeyUnwrapper.java:44-47.
rejected_leads.reason: Looks like a hardening/observable-timing concern rather than a source-proven vulnerability; no evidence in this snapshot that it is the case's fix target, and the prompt warns that a hardening opportunity is not by itself a vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: PKCS1Encoding.decodeBlock (pLen == -1) is not the constant-time path; in the non-default 'org.bouncycastle.pkcs1.not_strict' mode a zero-length/short decrypted block can reach data[0] / negative indexes (core/src/main/java/org/bouncycastle/crypto/encodings/PKCS1Encoding.java:354-419, 309-348).
rejected_leads.reason: Default configuration (useStrictLength=true) routes short blocks through blockBuffer and the fixed-length decodeBlockOrRandom path is constant time, so I could not demonstrate a usable padding oracle or exception oracle in the default configuration.

rejected_leads.lead: SM2Engine.notEncrypted compares every ciphertext byte against in[inOff] instead of in[inOff + i] (core/src/main/java/org/bouncycastle/crypto/engines/SM2Engine.java:182-193).
rejected_leads.reason: Real correctness defect, but the only consequence is an incorrect 'is the KDF output all zero' retry decision with negligible probability; no credible security impact.

rejected_leads.lead: JsseDefaultHostnameAuthorizer.isValidNameMatch wildcard prefix test uses prefix.indexOf('.') > 0 so a wildcard can match a name whose first label is empty (pkix/src/main/java/org/bouncycastle/est/jcajce/JsseDefaultHostnameAuthorizer.java:194-200).
rejected_leads.reason: Release notes already record an off-by-one fix in this method, invalid DNS names are required to exercise the residual case, and the verifier input is normally not attacker-controlled; too speculative to report.
The name is used with the DNS JNDI context factory and the domain value is application-supplied; no clear attacker-controlled injection sink comparable to the LDAP CertStore path.

summary: Reviewed the assigned bc-java snapshot (provider version "v1.60b", 1.60-dev release notes; tests excluded). Scope focus was attacker-controlled input reaching trust boundaries and security-sensitive transformations in core/prov/pkix/tls/pg. The single strongest source-evidenced candidate is an LDAP filter injection in the LDAP CertStore/Store implementations: values taken from X509CertSelector/X509CRLSelector subjects/issuers are concatenated into LDAP search filters without any escaping, and the resulting filter is executed with the application's LDAP connection. I could not identify a concrete root cause for the RSA/Bleichenbacher variants I considered (the constant-time PKCS#1 decode and TLS premaster fallbacks are present), so those remain unconfirmed leads rather than candidates. No code was executed and no upstream diff/CVE mapping was available in-scope.
